title: Northstar: a small customer's migration
disclosure: Synthetic interview — fictional company and speaker

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: How did your small Northstar deployment migrate?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: Our small deployment moved in six weeks because we used only standard connectors.

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: We had twelve users and did not maintain custom integrations. This was one migration, not a representative survey.

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: I cannot estimate how an enterprise deployment would compare.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: Can you describe a key preparation task and any uncertainties involved?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: One important preparation task was verifying all user accounts were active and correctly assigned before migration. We had to hand off this responsibility to our IT coordinator, who cross-checked the user list against active directory records. An uncertainty arose because some users had recently changed roles, and it wasn’t clear if their permissions matched their new responsibilities. We worked around this by scheduling a quick review meeting with department heads to confirm access needs. However, I could not observe the full accuracy of this review, so some mismatches might have persisted unnoticed.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: How did you implement recordkeeping during migration and handle any limitations?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: During the migration, we kept detailed logs of each step in a shared document accessible to the team. Since the migration was small, this manual recordkeeping worked well. However, a limitation was that some automatic system messages were not captured in the document, so we relied on memory and email confirmations to fill gaps. As a workaround, we designated a team member to summarize daily progress and issues. Still, I could not observe all behind-the-scenes system alerts, so some minor events might have gone unrecorded.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: How might a colleague misunderstand your local migration process and its limits?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: A colleague new to the project assumed that our migration logs captured every system event automatically. I explained that our logs were manually maintained and did not include all system-generated alerts. This misunderstanding could lead to overconfidence in the completeness of our records. I clarified that some issues might not appear in the logs and that informal communication was necessary to catch unlogged problems. This helped set realistic expectations about the limits of our documentation during the migration.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: Did you face any challenges arranging shared workspaces or labeling storage?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: Yes, organizing our shared workspace was tricky because different teams preferred different labeling styles for storage bins. We handed off the labeling task to the office manager, who created a compromise system using color codes and simple tags. The workaround was to keep a printed reference sheet near the storage area to explain the codes. However, some team members still found the system confusing, and I couldn’t observe how consistently labels were applied during busy days.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: How did you manage meeting agendas or shared stationery during the migration?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: Managing meeting agendas was occasionally inconvenient because different team leads had varying expectations on agenda detail. We handed off agenda compilation to the project coordinator, who used a shared digital document to gather input. For shared stationery, we kept a communal supply box, but it was often disorganized. The workaround was to assign someone weekly to reorder and tidy supplies. Despite this, the lack of a formal tracking system meant occasional shortages occurred, and I could not observe all usage patterns to prevent this fully.

turns.speaker: Moderator
turns.text: Can you give an example of passing a task to a colleague while noting observation limits?

turns.speaker: Fictional operator
turns.text: I once passed the responsibility for verifying data backups to a colleague before migration. I explained the task clearly and provided documentation on the backup schedules. However, I noted that I could not directly observe their verification process or confirm the backups’ integrity beyond their reports. The colleague encountered some unexpected file permission issues, which they resolved independently. This handoff worked well overall, but the limits of my observation meant I had to trust their judgment and follow up later to ensure everything was in order.
